transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~46m | Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood Product), Sarah Kim (Quantix Head of ML), Omar Reed (Quantix Platform), Maya Lopez (Quantix Security), Evan Chu (Quantix PO)

[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, um i'm lena from redwood inference, i'll kick us off. quick agenda -- structured output JSON mode, function/tool calling demo, quick console walkthrough and then q&a. sound good?
[00:18] Sarah Kim: yes thanks lena, excited we sent the example payloads earlier, hope you had a chance to look. main thing for us is deterministic output for our product catalog enrichment pipeline.
[00:30] Marco Diaz: yep saw the payloads, thanks sarah. we'll show JSON schemas and the guardrails we use to reduce hallucinations and invalid outputs. we'll also demo tool-calling to attach lookups and enrichments so the model returns a structured object plus api calls can be invoked automatically.
[00:48] Omar Reed: quick infra note — we need to understand hosted vs dedicated capacity because traffic will be spiky around promo windows; also data residency (eu/us) and KMS for secrets.
[01:02] Priya Singh: we'll cover those briefly; priya here on product. also will show optimize recommendations for batching/caching which often reduces per-token cost a lot.

[05:12] Marco Diaz: alright i'm going to share my screen — starting with the API flow. first: you can pass a json schema in the request body (we call it structured_output_schema) and set mode=json_schema. the model will try to produce valid json that fits schema. note: sometimes the transcription might show it as json-mode or jason-mode in logs — small typo in some agents — but it's the same param.
[05:43] Sarah Kim: how strict is the enforcement? if it drifts and returns a string or extra fields what's the typical behavior?
[05:55] Marco Diaz: good question. enforcement has two layers: 1) schema validation on the server side — we can auto-retry generation with constraints if the first output fails, and 2) a lightweight classifier/guard that flags fields that look hallucinated (e.g., invented SKUs). you can set strict=true to reject any non-conforming outputs, or strict=warn to accept and log.
[06:20] Maya Lopez: are those logs sent to our account or to redwood? we need audit logs for compliance.
[06:27] Marco Diaz: audit logs are stored under your account; we support long retention add-ons. also we integrate with your KMS/HSM for keying and we log access through SSO (SAML/Okta). i'll note that in the security doc.

[09:05] Marco Diaz: demo time - here's a simple schema for a product object: {id:string, title:string, price:float, attributes: array of {k:string,v:string}}. i'm going to call function-calling after generation to run a price-normalization tool we register as a server-side tool. you'll see how the model returns the function call payload.
[09:46] Sarah Kim: are tools run in our VPC or in redwood hosted infra?
[09:53] Marco Diaz: tools can be run in two ways — hosted webhooks on Redwood or in private deployments we install a lightweight agent in your VPC that calls back to your internal endpoints. for high-security setups you can require tool execution only inside your network.
[10:20] Evan Chu: for price normalization we also need rounding rules per region and tax-awareness. can that be encoded?
[10:28] Marco Diaz: yes you can pass region/tax config to the tool and the model can call it with structured args. example in the demo now.

[13:00] [screen noise] Marco Diaz: ok you can see model generated a function_call: name: "normalize_price", args: {price: "$1,299", region: "EU"} — sometimes the transcriber shows it as "function calling" or "function-calling" in the logs but that's just formatting. the key is the payload is valid JSON and we surface the function call as a first-class artifact in the response.
[13:36] Sarah Kim: what about streaming? we need to stream partial JSON for low-latency UIs.
[13:44] Marco Diaz: we support streaming structured output — we stream chunks that are JSON tokens; the console shows partials and a final checksum. caveat: partials may not be schema-valid until complete, but we do heuristics to show a best-effort partial object.

[17:05] Priya Singh: switching to the console — under Optimize suggestions you'll see a recommended batching window and whether to enable prefix KV caching for those identical product descriptions. for example with our retail workloads we often recommend a small prefix cache for catalog enrichment which cuts 30-40% token cost on repeated product descriptions.
[17:38] Omar Reed: is KV cache safe for PII? some of our descriptions include seller-specific tags we cannot cache outside of region.
[17:47] Priya Singh: yes, you can scope caches to tenant and region and set TTLs; for regulated data you can disable caching or restrict to private deployment. we'll include those options in the config file when we share the template.

[21:00] Marco Diaz: back to strictness — when strict=true we return an http 422 if the final json fails validation. we also provide an automatic fallback to a simpler schema or to a human review queue (we'll integrate with your internal ticketing via webhook).
[21:25] Sarah Kim: what's the expected latency penalty for strict validation and re-rolls?
[21:33] Marco Diaz: depends on model and batching. on hosted with a 1-2 token-length output it's usually +50-150ms for a re-roll. for longer outputs or if we call external tools it adds network time. for our dedicated pools you can pin smaller models that reduce re-roll RT to ~30-60ms.

[25:10] Maya Lopez: security — we need SOC2, iso27001, and encryption at rest/in-transit, plus KMS integration and audit logs. also SSO and RBAC for our dev and prod teams.
[25:25] Priya Singh: we are SOC2 Type II, we support ISO in roadmap (if this is a hard requirement we can share timelines), we integrate with customer KMS for private deployments and support SAML/Okta + SCIM for provisioning. i'll put links to the compliance pack in the follow-up.
[25:46] Maya Lopez: and do you support customer-managed keys for hosted?
[25:51] Marco Diaz: yes for hosted we can either bring your KMS or rotate a key we hold in a dedicated HSM instance per-customer (enterprise plan). for private deployments you always manage keys.

[29:00] Sarah Kim: quick question on cost — our CFO wants to compare per-conversation cost to Anthropic / OpenAI. do you have benchmark numbers?
[29:12] Lena Park: we have publicized benchmarks for common models and we'll run a custom bench for your payloads. typically our per-token costs are competitive and Optimize recommendations (batching + quantization) reduce unit cost further. i'll include a pricing example for a 3-month pilot.

[32:40] Marco Diaz: demo of function chaining — model returns product object, then calls a "lookup_inventory" tool that queries your inventory db. in hosted mode the tool call is proxied to your webhook; in private it's a local call. sometimes transcriptions show 'look-up inventory' or 'lookup in ven tree' — ignore that, it's the same action.
[33:15] Omar Reed: latency to inventory will be the big factor; can we run the tool inside our VPC?
[33:22] Marco Diaz: yes, that is the private agent case. we deploy an agent that accepts signed requests from Redwood, runs the tool against your internal endpoints, and returns results. no traffic leaves your VPC except the signed response.

[36:30] Marco Diaz: about model variants — we surface curated open models and redwood-verified perf profiles. you can route production traffic to a cheaper quantized variant and fallback to a larger model on failures. this is helpful during promos where you need graceful degradation.
[36:55] Sarah Kim: can routing be policy-driven by region or by latency SLA?
[37:02] Marco Diaz: yes — you can create policies in the console: route-by-latency, route-by-cost, or route-by-region. automatic fallback and canary policies are supported.

[39:45] Evan Chu: our timeline: want a small pilot in april and then scale if results look good. what does onboarding look like?
[39:56] Lena Park: typical onboarding: 1) pilot contract + reserved test capacity, 2) shared security review, 3) run benchmarks on samples, 4) two-week pilot with dedicated support and weekly syncs. we'll assign a CSM if you go pilot.

[42:10] Marco Diaz: quick note on observability — the console gives token-level cost breakdowns per endpoint, model-level latency distributions, and traces you can export to jaeger. also we tie evals to prompt sets so you can alert on quality regressions.
[42:35] Maya Lopez: export to our SIEM? we need log forwarding.
[42:40] Marco Diaz: yes we support log forwarding and webhook sinks; we'll include the spec.

[44:00] Lena Park: ok quick recap and next steps: we'll send pilot pricing and plan (Lena), security docs (Priya), Marco will run the hosted benchmark with your sample payloads, and Omar you'll confirm firewall/VPN details. schedule follow-up deep dive for dedicated infra week of 3/15. any final q's?
[44:25] Sarah Kim: no, that's great. thanks everyone.
[44:33] Maya Lopez: thanks, appreciate the compliance details.
[44:38] Lena Park: thanks all, we'll follow up over email.

Notes on transcription: some proper nouns and product names mis-transcribed (e.g., 'Redwood Optimize' shown as 'Redwood Opti-mize' in auto notes), occasional missing punctuation, and speaker attribution sometimes simplified to first names.
